meta.headline: South Korea's semiconductor exports just tripled year-over-year. Is it too much of a good thing?

relevance.reason: The article shows a country specialising in one export, the benefits for growth and the risks of dependence, which suits Theme 4 trade topics.

mapping.justification: The article is about South Korea's dependence on semiconductor exports, which raises the benefits and risks of specialisation.
mapping.cross_theme_note: The article spans Theme 4 (specialisation and pattern of trade) and Theme 2 (net trade as part of aggregate demand, interest rates and growth).

paragraphs: South Korea's chip exports have pushed overall exports to record levels. Semiconductor exports jumped 209% from a year earlier to $46.65 billion in August, accounting for 47.5% of total goods exports of $98.25 billion. The trade ministry said the increase was mainly caused by demand for AI infrastructure, as large cloud providers such as Google and Amazon increased their spending.

One analyst estimated that chips accounted for nearly 80% of export growth in August. Some economists worry about what happens if the boom fades. An economist at Moody's Analytics said a gradual slowdown would be manageable but an abrupt stall would be more serious, because the economy already runs at two speeds and the sectors that would need to take up the slack are under pressure.

There are other concerns. Car exports fell 29.8% in August, although the ministry blamed holiday timing and partial strikes for much of this. US tariffs and a move to produce in American plants are longer-lasting challenges. The Bank of Korea has raised its base rate to 3%, its second consecutive increase, because core inflation remains high, which could limit support if the chip cycle turns.

There are also reasons for optimism. The central bank says the recovery in consumption is gradually speeding up, and exports outside semiconductors grew 20%. An analyst at Lombard Odier said South Korea could still grow by around 2% to 3% a year if chips slowed but other sectors did well, and did not describe the economy as over-reliant on chips.

Specialising in a product with strong global demand can boost exports, output and incomes, but it also exposes a country to changes in that one market. This article shows the trade-off between the gains from specialisation and the risks of depending on a single sector, and how interest rates and other industries affect the outcome.

Risks of over-specialisation and the case for diversification

chain: South Korea specialises in semiconductors, and global spending on AI infrastructure lifts demand.
Export revenue jumps, raising net trade, aggregate demand, output and incomes.

evaluation.label: Speed of change
evaluation.text: a gradual slowdown in chip demand is manageable, but an abrupt stall would be more damaging.

evaluation.label: Other sectors
evaluation.text: non-semiconductor exports grew 20% and analysts still expect growth of around 2% to 3% if chips slow, so the risk may be smaller than it first appears.

evaluation.label: Short run and long run
evaluation.text: the boom helps growth now, but long-term stability depends on other industries, such as cars, recovering.

key_terms.definition: A material used to make computer chips, which are essential components in electronic goods and AI equipment.
When a country or firm concentrates on producing the goods it makes most efficiently and trades for the rest.
When a country can produce a good at a lower opportunity cost than another country.
Goods and services produced in one country and sold to buyers in other countries.
When an economy depends too heavily on one product or sector, so it is vulnerable if demand for it falls.
Spreading production and exports across many different sectors to reduce risk.
The total planned spending on an economy's goods and services, made up of consumption, investment, government spending and net exports.
The main interest rate set by a central bank, which influences borrowing and saving costs.

questions.prompt: Semiconductors made up $46.65bn of South Korea's $98.25bn of goods exports in August. What was the value of exports other than semiconductors?
questions.explanation: 98.25 − 46.65 = 51.60, so exports other than semiconductors were $51.60bn.

questions.prompt: What is the main risk to South Korea of relying heavily on semiconductor exports?

options.text: Imports will rise faster than exports
The economy is vulnerable if demand for chips falls
It will no longer earn foreign currency

questions.explanation: When one product makes up almost half of exports, a fall in demand for it can sharply reduce export revenue and growth.

questions.prompt: Other things equal, how would a rise in South Korea's exports affect its aggregate demand?

options.text: It rises, because net exports increase
It falls, because exports reduce spending
It stays the same, because exports are not part of AD
It falls, because imports must rise

questions.explanation: Net trade (exports minus imports) is a component of aggregate demand, so higher exports raise AD.

questions.prompt: Explain one risk for a country that depends on one sector for nearly half of its exports.

points: Identifies that the economy is vulnerable if demand for that sector's product falls.
Uses the article, for example semiconductors making up 47.5% of South Korea's goods exports or chips accounting for nearly 80% of export growth in August.

Develops a chain, for example: if global demand for chips stalls, export revenue falls sharply (1), so net trade, output and incomes fall and other struggling sectors such as cars cannot make up the difference (1).

notes: Award 1 mark for a partial chain and 2 for a complete one.

questions.prompt: Assess whether South Korea's reliance on semiconductor exports is a strength or a weakness for its economy.

points: Specialisation can raise output and export earnings.
Exports are part of aggregate demand.
Over-specialisation exposes an economy to shocks.
Bank of Korea base rate raised to 3%.
For strength: strong global demand raises export revenue, growth and incomes, and the AI boom shows comparative advantage.
For weakness: dependence on one sector leaves the economy exposed if demand or prices fall, other sectors are struggling, and rising interest rates limit the central bank's ability to support demand.
Judge using whether a slowdown would be gradual or abrupt, how well the other sectors perform, analysts' expectation of growth of around 2% to 3% even if chips slow, and the time period considered.
A supported conclusion might be that it is a strength now but a risk unless the economy diversifies.

discussion.prompt: Is it better for a country to specialise in what it does best or to spread its risk across many industries?

points.label: Moody's Analytics
points.text: A gradual slowdown would be manageable, but an abrupt stall is different, because the economy runs at two speeds and other sectors are under pressure.
